content.text: Web services are important because they:

items: Enable communication between applications built on different platforms and languages
Use open standards (e.g., HTTP, XML, JSON) to ensure interoperability
Promote reusability and modularity in software architecture
Support scalable and distributed system designs
Facilitate integration with third-party services and legacy systems
Software components that expose functionality over a network (usually HTTP)
Designed to allow machine-to-machine interaction over the web
Based on standards like SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) or REST (Representational State Transfer)
Capable of exchanging data in common formats such as XML and JSON
Typically used in modern applications to create loosely coupled, service-oriented architectures

content.text: Spring REST is a part of the Spring Framework that simplifies the development of RESTful web services. It leverages Spring’s core features such as dependency injection and component scanning to build scalable and maintainable REST APIs with minimal boilerplate.

items: Built on top of the Spring MVC framework
Supports HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, DELETE for RESTful operations
Uses annotations like @RestController, @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, etc.
Automatically handles request and response serialization (e.g., to/from JSON)
Easily integrates with other Spring modules (Security, Data, Boot, etc.)
Promotes separation of concerns through controller-service-repository layers
Marks a class as a web controller in Spring MVC.
Typically used in traditional web applications where views (like JSP) are returned.
Can be combined with @ResponseBody to return data instead of a view.
Indicates that the return value of a method should be bound to the web response body.
Used to send objects (e.g., JSON or XML) directly to the client.
Often used with @Controller to create RESTful behavior.
A convenience annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody.
Simplifies the creation of REST APIs by eliminating the need to annotate each method with @ResponseBody.
Commonly used for RESTful services that return data instead of views.
Maps HTTP requests to handler methods or controller classes.
Can be used at the class or method level.
Supports method attributes (GET, POST, etc.), URL paths, headers, and more.
Binds the HTTP request body to a method parameter.
Commonly used to deserialize JSON or XML input into a Java object.
Essential for handling incoming data in POST or PUT requests.
Maps HTTP GET requests to a specific handler method.
Typically used for retrieving data (e.g., fetching resources).
Example: @GetMapping("/users") maps to a method that returns a list of users.
Maps HTTP POST requests to a method.
Commonly used for creating new resources.
Example: @PostMapping("/users") maps to a method that creates a new user.
Maps HTTP PUT requests to a method.
Used to update an existing resource entirely.
Example: @PutMapping("/users/{id}") updates the user with the specified ID.
Maps HTTP DELETE requests to a method.
Used to remove a resource.
Example: @DeleteMapping("/users/{id}") deletes the user with the given ID.
Specifies the media types that a controller method or class can produce in the response.
Controls the Content-Type header of the HTTP response.
Common values include "application/json", "application/xml", "text/plain".

Example: @GetMapping(value = "/users", produces = "application/json")
public List<User> getUsers() { ... }
Specifies the media types that a controller method or class can consume from the request body.
Controls the expected Content-Type header of the HTTP request.
Common values include "application/json", "application/xml".

Example: @PostMapping(value = "/users", consumes = "application/json")
public void addUser(@RequestBody User user) { ... }
Used to bind a method parameter to a URI template variable.
Extracts values directly from the URL path.

Example: @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public User getUserById(@PathVariable("id") Long userId) { ... }
Used to bind a method parameter to a query parameter or form parameter in the request URL.
Extracts values from the URL’s query string or POST form data.

Example: @GetMapping("/users")
public List<User> getUsersByRole(@RequestParam("role") String role) { ... }
Used to trigger validation on a method parameter (usually a model or DTO).
Works with Java Bean Validation (JSR-380) annotations like @NotNull, @Size, etc.
Typically used in controller methods to validate incoming request bodies.

Example: @PostMapping("/users")
public ResponseEntity<?> createUser(@Valid @RequestBody User user) { ... }
Similar to @Valid, but allows grouping of validation constraints.
Can be applied at class level or method level to activate group-based validation.
Useful for more advanced validation scenarios.

Example: @Validated(OnCreate.class)
public void createUser(@RequestBody User user) { ... }
A specialized version of @ControllerAdvice that combines @ControllerAdvice and @ResponseBody.
Allows centralized exception handling across all @RestController classes.
Enables defining global exception handling logic in one place.
Used within @RestControllerAdvice (or controllers) to define methods that handle specific exceptions.
Maps exceptions to custom response entities or messages.
RestTemplate is a synchronous client provided by Spring to consume RESTful web services easily.
It simplifies making HTTP requests and handling responses without manually managing connections.
getForObject(String url, Class<T> responseType)
postForObject(String url, Object request, Class<T> responseType)
put() — for HTTP PUT requests (updates)
delete() — for HTTP DELETE requests
exchange() — for executing requests with more control over HTTP method, headers, etc.
The version number is included as part of the URL path.
Example: GET /api/v1/users
Easy to implement and very explicit, but can lead to duplicated endpoints.
The version is specified as a query parameter.
Example: GET /api/users?version=1
Flexible, but versioning is less visible in the URL structure.
The version is passed via a custom HTTP header (e.g., X-API-Version).
Example: X-API-Version: 1
Keeps the URL clean but requires clients to set custom headers.
The version is specified in the Accept header using media types.
Example: Accept: application/vnd.company.app-v1+json
Allows for fine-grained version control but can be more complex to manage.

Embedded servers like Tomcat or Jetty—no need for external server deployment
